text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Former Prime Minister Carl Bildt, who was expected to return to Swedish politics next year, could remain in Bosnia as EU High Commissioner or peace maker. Bildt says he is under pressure to stay and even the Clinton administration, which criticised Bildt a year ago, wants him to continue his work.
- Sweden lost the Davis Cup to France after Nicklas Kulti lost the fourth match point to Arnaud Boetsch in the fifth and final game.
- Swedish biotechnological researchers will get 300 million kronor to create new companies out of research projects.
- More older people will be cared for at home as 17 percent of capcity within institutions is cut.

- Women are dissatisfied with Prime Minister Goran Persson's way of heading the government, a new poll showed. Women in the trade union movement have lost confidence in Persson's Social Democrats party, but there is also dissatisfaction among top Social Democrats politicians.

- President of car retailer Catena, Mats Jansson, believes there will be a boost in Volvo's car sales in 1997 due to new rules for company cars. But Jansson said 1996 will be tough for Volvo as well as the entire Swedish car retail sales sector.
- The world's biggest fund manager, American Fidelity Investments, opens its office in Sweden. Sparbanken has already started selling Fidelity funds.
- IKEA is opening five new stores in Italy between now and the year 2000. Over the past five years its sales in Italy have risen by 183 percent.
